meta.purpose: Sample items for building UI for three NGN types not yet rendered.

types.highlight_text: Render `passage` as inline segments joined by a space. Each segment is clickable and toggles a yellow highlight. `select` is how many are correct. Score +/-: one point per correct segment, minus one per wrong. Each segment carries its own rationale for review.
types.highlight_list: Same interaction as highlight_text but `options` render as a bulleted list instead of prose. The stem states how many to pick; `select` is that count. Enforce at most `select` highlights.
types.matrix_multi: Checkbox grid. `columns` are the headers, `rows` are the findings. Each row's `answer` is an ARRAY, so a finding may belong to more than one column. Existing `matrix` items in questions.json use a STRING answer and are single-select, so branch on Array.isArray(row.answer).

questions.stem: For each nurse activity, select every ANA standard category it demonstrates. An activity may belong to more than one.

rows.text: Completing an admission assessment on a new patient
rows.rationale: Assessment is the first Standard of Practice, the nursing process steps.

rows.text: Reviewing current literature before revising a unit protocol
rows.rationale: Evidence-based practice and research is a Standard of Professional Performance.

rows.text: Precepting a newly licensed nurse and evaluating that nurse's growth
rows.rationale: Covers both education and professional practice evaluation, both Performance standards.

rows.text: Writing measurable outcomes with the patient, then reassessing whether they were met
rows.rationale: Outcomes identification and evaluation are both Standards of Practice.

rows.text: Coordinating a discharge plan with physical therapy and social work
rows.rationale: Coordination of care is a Standard of Practice, and collaboration is a Standard of Professional Performance. This row is the reason the item allows more than one column.

questions.takeaway: Standards of Practice follow the nursing process. Standards of Professional Performance describe how the nurse behaves as a professional.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the activity is a step in caring for this patient or a statement about the nurse's professional conduct. Coordination sits in both.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old with heart failure is being discharged after a third admission in four months. He lives alone, has no car, and tells the nurse he sometimes splits his pills to make the prescription last.
questions.stem: Highlight the three (3) findings that most support a referral to case management.

options.text: Third admission in four months
options.rationale: Readmission patterns are the classic trigger for case management involvement.

options.text: Reports splitting pills to make the prescription last
options.rationale: Cost-related nonadherence is a resource problem case management exists to solve.

options.text: Prefers tea to coffee in the morning
options.rationale: A preference with no bearing on discharge safety.

options.text: No transportation to follow-up appointments
options.rationale: Access to follow-up is a named determinant of readmission.

options.text: Has a daughter who calls twice weekly
options.rationale: A support, not a gap. It weighs against the need for referral.

options.text: Weighs himself most mornings
options.rationale: Evidence of self-management, which is what discharge teaching aims for.

questions.takeaway: Case management targets the gaps that drive readmission: cost, transportation, and repeat admissions.
questions.strategy: Sort each item into barrier or strength. Only barriers support a referral.

questions.scenario: An 84-year-old was admitted three days ago for a hip fracture. The nurse reads the night shift note.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up.

passage.text: Client admitted three days ago following a mechanical fall at home.
passage.rationale: Background history, already known and being treated.

passage.text: Oriented to person only tonight, having been oriented x 3 on admission.
passage.rationale: An acute change in orientation is the defining feature of delirium.

passage.text: Wears reading glasses and a hearing aid.
passage.rationale: Sensory changes are expected with aging and are not new.

passage.text: Pulling at the intravenous line and attempting to climb out of bed.
passage.rationale: New agitation plus a fall risk in a client already admitted for a fracture.

passage.text: Received a sedative at 2200 for sleep.
passage.rationale: Sedatives are a named contributor to delirium in older adults.

passage.text: Family reports she reads the newspaper daily at home.
passage.rationale: Establishes a high cognitive baseline, which makes the change meaningful, but is not itself a finding to act on.

passage.text: No bowel movement since admission.
passage.rationale: Constipation and urinary retention are reversible contributors that are easy to miss.

passage.text: Temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 78, blood pressure 132/76.
passage.rationale: All within normal limits.

questions.takeaway: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and caused by something. Look for the cause rather than treating the agitation.
questions.strategy: Highlight only what is new or reversible. Chronic and baseline findings are distractors.

questions.stem: For each nurse action, select every domain it supports. An action may support more than one.

rows.text: Asking the client which name and pronouns to use, then recording them in the chart
rows.rationale: Signals respect and ensures every later interaction uses correct information.

rows.text: Collecting an organ inventory rather than assuming based on gender marker
rows.rationale: Determines which screenings apply. A transgender man may still need cervical screening.

rows.text: Asking about a partner without assuming the partner's gender
rows.rationale: Avoids forcing a correction and captures the real support system.

rows.text: Discussing gender identity only where the conversation cannot be overheard
rows.rationale: Disclosure carries real risk. Controlling who hears it is part of safety.

rows.text: Sharing a client's transgender status with staff not involved in their care
rows.rationale: Supports no domain. This is a privacy violation. A row with no correct column tests whether the UI allows an all-empty row.

questions.takeaway: Affirming care is not only kindness. Accurate identity and anatomy data change which screenings a client receives.
questions.strategy: Ask what each action accomplishes. Several accomplish more than one thing, and one accomplishes nothing.

questions.stem: For each activity, select the level of prevention it represents.

rows.text: Administering an influenza vaccine to a well adult
rows.rationale: Prevents the disease before it occurs.

rows.text: Screening mammography for a woman with no symptoms
rows.rationale: Early detection in someone who has no symptoms yet.

rows.text: Cardiac rehabilitation after a myocardial infarction
rows.rationale: Limits disability and prevents further decline after disease is established.

rows.text: Teaching foot care to a client with diagnosed diabetes
rows.rationale: The disease exists. This prevents ulceration and amputation, a complication.

rows.text: A community blood pressure screening event that also hands out low-sodium recipes
rows.rationale: Screening is secondary, and the dietary teaching is primary prevention for those who screen normal.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents, secondary detects, tertiary limits damage already done.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the disease is absent, present but silent, or present and established.

questions.scenario: A nurse is assigned to a client who is frightened before a first chemotherapy infusion.
questions.stem: Highlight the three (3) actions that best demonstrate caring presence.

options.text: Sitting at eye level and allowing silence while the client cries
options.rationale: Presence means being with the client, not fixing the feeling.

options.text: Telling the client not to worry because most people tolerate it well
options.rationale: False reassurance closes the conversation.

options.text: Asking what the client is most afraid of
options.rationale: Knowing the client is a core caring behavior and directs everything after it.

options.text: Completing the infusion checklist efficiently without interrupting
options.rationale: Competent, but task focused rather than a caring behavior.

options.text: Explaining each step before doing it and pausing for questions
options.rationale: Comforting through predictability, which reduces the fear of the unknown.

options.text: Offering to call the chaplain instead of continuing the conversation
options.rationale: Referral can be appropriate later, but here it hands off the moment rather than staying in it.

questions.takeaway: Caring is measured by presence and knowing the client, not by reassurance or efficiency.
questions.strategy: Reject anything that ends the conversation. Caring behaviors keep it open.

questions.scenario: A 54-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the clinic. The nurse documents the following.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate an exacerbation rather than the client's usual state.

passage.text: Client reports chronic morning cough productive of clear sputum for several years.
passage.rationale: The baseline for this client, stated as long-standing.

passage.text: Sputum has been thick and green for the past two days.
passage.rationale: A change in sputum color and consistency signals infection.

passage.text: Normally walks to the mailbox without stopping, now stops twice.
passage.rationale: A decline measured against the client's own baseline, which is what exacerbation means.

passage.text: Uses two pillows at night, as he has for years.
passage.rationale: Unchanged, so it is baseline rather than acute.

passage.text: Using accessory muscles at rest.
passage.rationale: Work of breathing at rest indicates the client is decompensating.

passage.text: Oxygen saturation 86% on room air, usually 92%.
passage.rationale: A six point drop from a stated personal baseline.

passage.text: Has smoked one pack daily for thirty years.
passage.rationale: A risk factor and a teaching opportunity, but not an acute finding.

passage.text: Barrel chest noted on inspection.
passage.rationale: A chronic structural change, present for years in advanced disease.

questions.takeaway: In chronic illness the abnormal finding is not the alarm. The change from that client's own baseline is.
questions.strategy: For every finding ask: is this new, or has it always been true for him? Only the new ones count.

questions.stem: For each action, select every principle it upholds.

rows.text: Using a professional interpreter rather than the client's teenage son
rows.rationale: Protects accuracy and confidentiality, and frees the client to speak openly about their own care.

rows.text: Asking the client what they believe caused the illness
rows.rationale: Treats this client as the authority on their own beliefs rather than assuming from background.

rows.text: Looking up the client's culture in a reference guide and following what it says
rows.rationale: Upholds none. Group generalizations applied to an individual are the definition of stereotyping.

rows.text: Speaking to the client directly while the interpreter translates
rows.rationale: Keeps the client as the participant rather than making the interpreter the conversation partner.

rows.text: Asking whether any practices around food or modesty should shape the plan of care
rows.rationale: An open question that gathers real data instead of assuming, and lets the client direct the plan.

questions.takeaway: Cultural competence is asking this client, not knowing facts about their group.
questions.strategy: Any option where the nurse assumes rather than asks upholds nothing.

questions.scenario: An 80-year-old comes to the clinic with her daughter for a routine visit.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that increase this client's risk of falling.

passage.text: Client lives alone in a two-story home and does her own cooking.
passage.rationale: Describes independence. Stairs alone are not a risk factor without impairment.

passage.text: Takes nine prescription medications including a diuretic and a benzodiazepine for sleep.
passage.rationale: Polypharmacy is a named risk, and both of those classes independently raise fall risk.

passage.text: Reports feeling dizzy when she stands up quickly.
passage.rationale: Orthostatic symptoms are a direct fall mechanism.

passage.text: Wears bifocals updated last year.
passage.rationale: Bifocals distort depth perception at stair edges and are a documented fall contributor.

passage.text: Daughter reports two loose throw rugs in the hallway.
passage.rationale: An environmental hazard and the most easily corrected item here.

passage.text: Attends a water aerobics class twice weekly.
passage.rationale: Exercise is protective and reduces fall risk.

passage.text: Blood pressure 138/78 seated.
passage.rationale: Acceptable, and a single seated reading does not show orthostatic change.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk is multifactorial: medications, sensory changes, orthostasis, and environment.
questions.strategy: Distractors here describe function and protective habits. Highlight only what makes a fall more likely.

questions.scenario: The nurse is preparing to call the provider about a postoperative client.
questions.stem: Highlight the three (3) highest priority findings to emphasize to the provider.

options.text: Amount of oral intake
options.rationale: Useful data, but not what changes management in the next minutes.

options.text: Blood pressure falling from 118/72 to 88/50
options.rationale: A falling pressure suggests hypovolemia or sepsis and demands action now.

options.text: Temperature rising from 37.1 C to 38.9 C
options.rationale: A rising fever with hypotension points toward sepsis.

options.text: New confusion in a previously alert client
options.rationale: Acute mental status change is an early and often first sign of deterioration.

options.text: Client's preference for a private room
options.rationale: Not clinical.

options.text: Dressing dry and intact
options.rationale: A normal finding. Normal findings do not drive a provider call.

questions.takeaway: Report the findings that are changing and that point to instability, not the ones that are stable.
questions.strategy: Highlight what is trending in the wrong direction. Normal and non-clinical items are distractors.

questions.scenario: The nurse cares for a newly admitted client in the Emergency department.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require intervention.

passage.text: Client brought to the Emergency department via ambulance.
passage.rationale: Mode of arrival, not a clinical finding.

passage.text: Client is alert and oriented x 3.
passage.rationale: A normal neurological finding.

passage.text: Reports pain 9 out of 10 in the right lower flank, radiating from the right upper quadrant to the mid and lower back for two days.
passage.rationale: Severe pain with a radiating pattern requires assessment and management now.

passage.text: States the pain has increased today over the past seven hours.
passage.rationale: A worsening trend, which changes urgency.

passage.text: Febrile at 38.8 C for the last 24 hours.
passage.rationale: Sustained fever with flank pain suggests infection.

passage.text: Reports vomiting episodes for 48 hours.
passage.rationale: Two days of vomiting risks dehydration and electrolyte loss.

passage.text: Denies dysuria, polyuria, and abdominal pain.
passage.rationale: Negative findings. They narrow the differential but need no intervention.

questions.takeaway: Findings that require intervention are abnormal, worsening, or threaten stability. Negatives and normals are neither.
questions.strategy: Read each sentence and ask whether it would change what you do in the next hour.

questions.scenario: A 72-year-old admitted with pneumonia has decreased mobility, poor intake, and a reddened sacrum.
questions.stem: For each assessment finding, select every nursing diagnosis it supports. A finding may support more than one.

rows.text: Oxygen saturation 88% on room air
rows.rationale: Direct evidence of inadequate oxygenation.

rows.text: Eating less than 25% of meals for four days
rows.rationale: Poor intake is nutritional data and is also a named risk factor for skin breakdown.

rows.text: Remains in bed, repositioning only with assistance
rows.rationale: Immobility drives pressure injury and also worsens atelectasis and gas exchange.

rows.text: Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum
rows.rationale: Nonblanchable redness is already a stage 1 pressure injury, the strongest single piece of evidence here.

rows.text: Serum albumin 2.6 g/dL
rows.rationale: Low albumin reflects poor protein status and predicts impaired healing.

questions.takeaway: One piece of assessment data often supports several diagnoses. That overlap is what the matrix format is testing.
questions.strategy: Take each finding across the row and ask separately whether it supports each column.

questions.stem: Highlight the three (3) statements that are correctly written client outcomes.

options.text: Client will ambulate 20 feet with a walker twice daily by postoperative day three.
options.rationale: Client centered, measurable, and time limited.

options.text: Encourage the client to ambulate in the hallway.
options.rationale: This is a nursing intervention, not an outcome. It describes what the nurse does.

options.text: Client will report pain of 3 or less on a 0 to 10 scale within 60 minutes of analgesic administration.
options.rationale: Specific, measurable, and bounded in time.

options.text: Client will understand the importance of incentive spirometry.
options.rationale: Understand cannot be measured. A correct version would say demonstrate or describe.

options.text: Client will demonstrate correct insulin self-injection before discharge.
options.rationale: Demonstrate is observable and the timeframe is defined.

options.text: Client will have adequate oxygenation.
options.rationale: Adequate is undefined, so two nurses could disagree on whether it was met.

questions.takeaway: An outcome describes what the client will do, in observable terms, by a stated time.
questions.strategy: Reject anything starting with a nurse verb, and anything using understand, adequate, or normal.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse is assigning tasks on a busy medical unit that includes assistive personnel.
questions.stem: Highlight the three (3) tasks that may be delegated to assistive personnel.

options.text: Obtaining routine vital signs on a stable client
options.rationale: A standardized task with a predictable outcome on a stable client.

options.text: Performing the admission assessment on a new client
options.rationale: Assessment cannot be delegated. It requires nursing judgment.

options.text: Assisting a client to the bathroom and recording output
options.rationale: Routine care and simple data collection within the scope of assistive personnel.

options.text: Teaching a client how to use an incentive spirometer
options.rationale: Teaching cannot be delegated.

options.text: Repositioning a client every two hours
options.rationale: A routine standardized task.

options.text: Evaluating whether a client's pain improved after medication
options.rationale: Evaluation is a nursing process step and stays with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Assessment, teaching, evaluation, and judgment never transfer. Routine standardized tasks on stable clients may.
questions.strategy: If the option starts with assess, teach, evaluate, or plan, it stays with the nurse.

questions.scenario: The outcome was: client will ambulate 20 feet with a walker twice daily by postoperative day three. It is now day three.
questions.stem: For each observation, select whether it shows the outcome was met, and whether it requires the plan to be revised. An observation may be both or neither.

rows.text: Client ambulated 25 feet with the walker twice today
rows.rationale: Exceeds the distance and meets the frequency. No revision needed.

rows.text: Client ambulated 20 feet once today and declined the second walk due to pain
rows.rationale: Partially met only. Pain is the barrier, so the plan needs a pain management step before ambulation.

rows.text: Client ambulated 20 feet twice but required two staff for balance
rows.rationale: The stated outcome was achieved, yet the assistance level reveals a safety problem the plan did not capture.

rows.text: Client refused to get out of bed both times
rows.rationale: Not met, and refusal needs its cause explored before the plan can work.

rows.text: Client ambulated to the bathroom independently without the walker
rows.rationale: Not met as written, and it is a safety concern rather than progress if the walker was ordered.

questions.takeaway: An outcome can be met and still leave a problem the plan must address.
questions.strategy: Evaluate against the outcome exactly as written, then ask separately whether anything new appeared.

questions.scenario: A nurse receives report on four clients at the start of the shift.
questions.stem: Highlight the three (3) clients the nurse should assess first.

options.text: A client with an oxygen saturation of 87% on 2 liters by nasal cannula
options.rationale: Airway and breathing come first, and this is a failing oxygenation.

options.text: A client requesting a bedpan
options.rationale: A comfort need that can be delegated.

options.text: A client with new onset chest pain rated 7 out of 10
options.rationale: New chest pain is potentially life threatening and time critical.

options.text: A client whose blood glucose is 48 mg/dL
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia progresses to seizure and loss of consciousness quickly.

options.text: A client asking when the provider will round
options.rationale: An information need, not a clinical priority.

options.text: A client due for a scheduled dressing change
options.rationale: Scheduled routine care that can wait.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize by threat to life: airway and breathing, then circulation, then anything that deteriorates quickly.
questions.strategy: Separate the unstable from the merely inconvenienced. Requests and scheduled tasks are almost never first.

questions.stem: For each situation, select every ethical principle involved. A situation may involve more than one.

rows.text: A competent client refuses a blood transfusion on religious grounds and the nurse honors it
rows.rationale: The client's right to decide, even against medical advice.

rows.text: Withholding a medication after noticing the dose ordered is ten times the safe range
rows.rationale: Prevents harm and acts in the client's interest.

rows.text: Allocating the last ICU bed by clinical need rather than by who arrived first
rows.rationale: Fair distribution of a scarce resource.

rows.text: Explaining risks and benefits fully so a client can decide about surgery
rows.rationale: Informed consent supports autonomy, and giving the information serves the client's good.

rows.text: Restraining a confused client for staff convenience
rows.rationale: Upholds nothing. It violates autonomy and nonmaleficence, which is different from supporting them.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy is the client deciding, beneficence is doing good, nonmaleficence is avoiding harm, justice is fairness.
questions.strategy: Ask which principle the action supports, not which it violates. A violating action supports none.

questions.stem: For each nurse action, select every category that applies.

rows.text: Documenting a medication as given before actually administering it
rows.rationale: Falsified documentation. No incident has occurred yet, but the record is now inaccurate.

rows.text: Administering a medication to the wrong client and notifying the provider
rows.rationale: An error occurred. Reporting it is correct, but the error itself carries liability.

rows.text: Questioning an illegible order before carrying it out
rows.rationale: The nurse is independently accountable for verifying orders.

rows.text: Discussing a client's condition in a crowded elevator
rows.rationale: A privacy breach under HIPAA.

rows.text: A client falls while ambulating with the nurse and is uninjured
rows.rationale: Any fall is reported regardless of injury. Being present and assisting means the standard was not breached.

questions.takeaway: An incident report documents an event. It is not an admission of wrongdoing, and the two do not always occur together.
questions.strategy: Ask separately whether an event happened, and whether the nurse acted below the standard.

questions.scenario: A client says quietly, I do not think this treatment is going to work.
questions.stem: Highlight the three (3) therapeutic responses.

options.text: You sound discouraged.
options.rationale: Reflection names the feeling and invites the client to continue.

options.text: Why would you say that?
options.rationale: Why questions demand justification and put the client on the defensive.

options.text: Tell me more about what you are thinking.
options.rationale: An open ended invitation that keeps control with the client.

options.text: Your doctor is excellent, so try not to worry.
options.rationale: False reassurance plus deflection to someone else.

options.text: Sitting down and remaining silent for a moment
options.rationale: Silence gives the client room to say the harder thing.

options.text: Everyone feels that way at first.
options.rationale: Minimizes this client's experience by generalizing it.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic responses open the conversation. Reassurance, why questions, and generalizations close it.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the client is likely to say more after this response. If not, it is not therapeutic.

questions.stem: For each teaching activity, select every learning domain it addresses.

rows.text: Client explains which foods raise blood glucose
rows.rationale: Knowledge and understanding.

rows.text: Client draws up and injects the correct insulin dose
rows.rationale: A performed skill.

rows.text: Client states willingness to check glucose before driving
rows.rationale: Attitude and values, the willingness to adopt a behavior.

rows.text: Client demonstrates foot inspection while explaining what changes to report
rows.rationale: A skill performed and knowledge stated at the same time.

rows.text: Client describes how diabetes has changed his view of himself and asks to join a support group
rows.rationale: Feelings and self concept, together with articulated understanding.

questions.takeaway: Cognitive is knowing, affective is feeling and valuing, psychomotor is doing. Real teaching often spans two.
questions.strategy: Look at the verb. Explain and describe are cognitive, demonstrate is psychomotor, and willingness is affective.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews a colleague's narrative note before the end of shift.
questions.stem: Highlight the portions of this note that do not meet documentation standards.

passage.text: 0800 Client reports pain 7 out of 10 in the right hip.
passage.rationale: Objective, quantified, and timed. This is correct documentation.

passage.text: Client appears to be drug seeking.
passage.rationale: A judgment, not an observation. Records opinion rather than fact.

passage.text: 0815 Hydromorphone 1 mg given intravenously.
passage.rationale: Drug, dose, route, and time are all present.

passage.text: Client was uncooperative during the dressing change.
passage.rationale: A label. Should describe the observed behavior instead.

passage.text: Error in the previous entry covered with correction fluid and rewritten.
passage.rationale: Never obscure an entry. Draw a single line, initial, and date it.

passage.text: 0900 Reassessed pain, client reports 3 out of 10.
passage.rationale: Correct follow-up documentation showing the response to the intervention.

passage.text: Charted at 1000 for care planned for 1400 so the shift would not run behind.
passage.rationale: Charting in advance is falsification, regardless of intent.

questions.takeaway: Document what you observed, when it happened, and only after it happened.
questions.strategy: Highlight anything that is an opinion, a label, an alteration, or written ahead of the event.

questions.scenario: A nurse meets with a client whose spouse died four months ago.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that suggest this client needs further intervention rather than expected grieving.

passage.text: Client cries when describing the spouse's last weeks.
passage.rationale: Expected grief. Crying about a loss is not pathology.

passage.text: Reports sleeping two to three hours nightly for the past two months.
passage.rationale: Sustained sleep deprivation is a physical consequence needing intervention.

passage.text: Has lost 20 pounds without trying.
passage.rationale: Significant unintentional weight loss signals the stress is causing physical harm.

passage.text: Keeps a photograph of the spouse on the bedside table.
passage.rationale: A normal act of remembrance.

passage.text: States there is no reason to keep going.
passage.rationale: A passive suicidal statement. This is the highest priority finding in the passage.

passage.text: Has stopped attending the weekly card game she previously enjoyed.
passage.rationale: Withdrawal from previously valued activities at four months suggests complicated grief.

passage.text: Talks with her daughter on the telephone most days.
passage.rationale: Maintained social connection, a protective factor.

questions.takeaway: Grief becomes a clinical problem when it produces physical harm, withdrawal, or hopelessness.
questions.strategy: Any statement suggesting the client sees no future is highlighted first, every time.

questions.scenario: A client reports difficulty falling asleep and describes a typical evening.
questions.stem: Highlight the habits that are interfering with this client's sleep.

passage.text: Goes to bed at approximately the same time each night.
passage.rationale: A consistent schedule supports sleep.

passage.text: Drinks two cups of coffee after dinner.
passage.rationale: Caffeine within six hours of bed delays sleep onset.

passage.text: Watches television in bed until falling asleep.
passage.rationale: Breaks the bed and sleep association, and the light suppresses melatonin.

passage.text: Keeps the bedroom cool and dark.
passage.rationale: Both are recommended.

passage.text: Takes a two-hour nap most afternoons.
passage.rationale: Long late naps reduce sleep drive at night.

passage.text: Has a glass of wine at bedtime to relax.
passage.rationale: Alcohol shortens sleep onset but fragments sleep and suppresses REM later in the night.

passage.text: Walks for 30 minutes each morning.
passage.rationale: Morning exercise improves sleep quality.

questions.takeaway: Caffeine, alcohol, long naps, and screens in bed are the four classic sleep hygiene violations.
questions.strategy: Alcohol is the trap. Clients describe it as helping, and it makes sleep worse.

questions.stem: For each finding, select every condition it is consistent with. A finding may support more than one.

rows.text: Diaphoresis and shakiness
rows.rationale: Adrenergic symptoms from the catecholamine response to falling glucose.

rows.text: Kussmaul respirations with fruity breath
rows.rationale: Deep rapid breathing blows off carbon dioxide to compensate for metabolic acidosis, and acetone gives the odor. Specific to DKA.

rows.text: Altered mental status
rows.rationale: Common to all three, which is why glucose is checked before anything else in a confused diabetic client.

rows.text: Serum glucose above 600 mg/dL with minimal ketones
rows.rationale: Residual insulin suppresses ketogenesis but not hyperglycemia, the defining difference from DKA.

rows.text: Polyuria and profound dehydration
rows.rationale: Osmotic diuresis occurs in both hyperglycemic states, and is most extreme in HHS.

rows.text: Typically occurs in type 1 diabetes
rows.rationale: Absolute insulin deficiency permits unrestrained lipolysis and ketone production.

questions.takeaway: Ketones separate DKA from HHS. Altered mental status separates none of them, so check a glucose first.
questions.strategy: Work column by column for the specific findings, then decide which rows belong to everything.
